newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU defies ministers' call for three-way fur ban.
newsitem.headline: EU defies ministers' call for three-way fur ban.

text.p: The European Commission rejected on Wednesday EU environment ministers' calls for a ban on fur imports from Canada, Russia and the United States as a way to force new talks on animal-trap standards.

The EU executive ignored the ministers' instructions to prepare the import ban against all three countries, preferring to recommend approval of a draft deal agreed with Canada and Russia while continuing work on a threatened ban against U.S. imports, a senior Commission official told Reuters.
"We are going to put to (EU member state officials) the draft deal with Canada and Russia," said the official, who asked not to be named.
"The Commission will carry on negotiating with the Americans in order to conclude a deal as soon as possible," he added.
Environment ministers asked the Commission to reopen talks with the three earlier this month "with a view to reaching a more satisfactory agreement" on standards for leg-hold and other animal traps.

Ministers were unhappy that the deal would ban only steel- jawed, leg-hold traps while leaving less clear the fate of padded traps, whose main difference compared with steel-jawed devices is that they carry rubber strips on their jaws.
The draft deal foresees standards for traps intended to kill or catch 18 species of wild animals, including muskrats, beavers, sable, lynx and wolves.
The Commission, by agreeing to present EU member states with the draft deal, is challenging governments to reject it formally if they don't like it.
Another Commission official said Wednesday's decision was a clear victory for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan over his environment counterpart Ritt Bjerregaard.

Brittan's officials had argued against preparing import bans against all three countries to try to force concessions, saying the draft deal was as good as could be expected and that such action risked sparking retaliatory action in the World Trade Organisation.
Sources close to Bjerregaard, who also requested anonymity, told Reuters the Dane had "dissociated" herself from Wednesday's decision, saying it was unacceptable on animal welfare grounds.

They said Bjerregaard would challenge Brittan to defend the decision himself before ministers and the European Parliament, some of whose members have vehemently attacked previous delays to the ban's enforcement.
EU officials on the bloc's committee on the Convention on Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) will tackle the issue on Thursday, the first official said.
